Note::join_flat¶

Back to Note API Reference

Signature¶

std::string Note::join_flat(std::string_view separator = " ") const

Materialize One Standard String¶

join_flat() copies all cells in row-major order into an owning std::string. It is the direct bridge to a standard C++ consumer that wants one contiguous character or byte sequence rather than another Note. Its default separator is one ASCII space; pass "" to concatenate without a boundary or another string to choose the boundary explicitly.

The method is shape-agnostic: scalars, vectors, matrices, and tensors are all read as the same flat sequence used by at(linear) and vector(). The returned string owns its bytes and remains valid after the source Note is destroyed. Embedded zero bytes are preserved because std::string and std::string_view are length-aware.

Unlike join(), join_flat() accepts both UTF-8 and bytes-mode Notes and returns no encoding tag. This makes it appropriate for assembling a binary payload, but the caller must remember whether the resulting string is text or arbitrary bytes. Zero cells yield an empty string. Undefined Notes reject because a standard string has no representation for an absent Note.

The method performs one result allocation strategy and copies O(total cell bytes + separator bytes). It does not mutate or decode the source.

Example 1: Use The Default Space¶

const auto words = pluss::note::make({"red", "green", "blue"});
std::cout << "default=" << words.join_flat() << '\n';

Output¶

default=red green blue

Example 2: Choose A Separator And Flatten A Matrix¶

const auto grid = pluss::note::make(
    std::vector<std::string>{"a", "b", "c", "d"},
    std::array<std::int64_t, 2>{2, 2});
std::cout << "custom=" << grid.join_flat("/") << '\n';

Output¶

custom=a/b/c/d

Passing "" is the standard-string counterpart of calling join() with no argument.

Example 3: The Result Owns Its Bytes¶

std::string retained;
{
  retained = pluss::note::make({"left", "right"}).join_flat("+");
}
std::cout << "lifetime=" << retained << '\n';

Output¶

lifetime=left+right

Example 4: Preserve Binary Zeros¶

const auto raw = pluss::note::bytes(
    std::vector<std::string>{std::string("A\0", 2), "B"},
    std::array<std::int64_t, 1>{2});
const auto joined = raw.join_flat("|");

std::cout << "raw size=" << joined.size() << " values="
          << static_cast<int>(static_cast<unsigned char>(joined[0])) << ','
          << static_cast<int>(static_cast<unsigned char>(joined[1])) << ','
          << static_cast<int>(static_cast<unsigned char>(joined[2])) << ','
          << static_cast<int>(static_cast<unsigned char>(joined[3])) << '\n';

Output¶

raw size=4 values=65,0,124,66

Example 5: Zero Cells Yield An Empty String¶

const auto empty = pluss::note::make(
    std::vector<std::string>{},
    std::array<std::int64_t, 2>{2, 0});
std::cout << "zero cells bytes=" << empty.join_flat(",").size() << '\n';

Output¶

zero cells bytes=0

Example 6: Undefined Rejects¶

try { (void)pluss::Note::undefined().join_flat(","); }
catch (const pluss::Error&) {
  std::cout << "join_flat undefined: rejected\n";
}

Output¶

join_flat undefined: rejected

See Also¶

  • join: return a scalar UTF-8 Note; default to no separator.

  • host: copy cells separately while retaining rank metadata.

  • vector: allocate only borrowed views, not copied bytes.
